{"id": "90:7/q12", "question": "How do surrounding verses and the sūra frame this question?", "turns_on": "The notes make different links: divine faculties and judgment, structural parallels and self-sufficiency, or the spending claim against the sūra's difficult moral path.", "positions": [{"id": "90:7/q12/p1", "position": "The paired questions and the ensuing gifts establish God's power to see, judge, and requite.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī say eyes, tongue and lips or the two eyes recall divine favor and prove power to account and resurrect. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 67:14: the creator of perception and speech knows and judges acts. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the eyes directly answer the assumption of being unseen; al-Tibyān says the creator who gave strength is more powerful and knows deeds. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ pairs future power and past surveillance across the human's full course and invokes 96:6–8 on arrogance, creation and return. Elmalılı also links gifts to power, knowledge and divergent souls."}, {"id": "90:7/q12/p2", "position": "The repeated questions bind the stanza and challenge imagined independence from God.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the second stanza resumes the introduction's human theme in two rhymed triplets, with repeated third-person polemical questions and matching openings and rhyme. It compares the self-sufficiency theme with 104:1–3, 80:5, 92:8 and 96:7 and the questioning with 75:3 and 75:36. Al-Biqāʿī treats concealment as a fourth carnal desire and says unfulfilled desires drive hardship; Iṣlāḥī describes conceit about self-earned status that breeds indifference to God and the Hereafter."}, {"id": "90:7/q12/p3", "position": "The spending boast is set against the harder moral paths and service to others.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says spending alone falls short of difficult servitude and solidarity with believers. Iṣlāḥī says the boasters should thank God and help the needy, while their accounts of personal and collective expenses excuse miserliness. He glosses mālan lubadā as much wealth. Al-Thaʿlabī reports three vocalizations of lubadan: Abū Jaʿfar doubles bāʾ as a collective of labid and rākiʿ; Mujāhid rounds both lām and bāʾ with light bāʾ, with heavy-matter and reclining-man usages; others have ḍamma on lām and fatḥa on light bāʾ as plural of heap or a non-derived singular. Al-Sāmarrāʾī calls najd a raised hard path matching the sūra's hardship, unlike easy sabīl; most commentators call the two paths good and evil, and a Prophetic report cautions against preferring evil, which he judges closer. Guidance shows the paths without guaranteeing the good destination, as 22:4 illustrates."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q01", "question": "What does the question 'Have We not made' convey?", "turns_on": "Ibn ʿĀshūr permits both assent and reproach; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attends to the contrast in tense.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q01/p1", "position": "It calls for assent to the fact that God made these faculties.", "reasons": "Elmalılı spells out the affirmative answer: yes, We made them. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a confirmatory question. Corpus Coranicum compares the ʾa-lam question in lists of divine favors in 93:6–8 and 94:1–4."}, {"id": "90:8/q01/p2", "position": "It reproaches and rejects the person's boast.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the question may reject the boast, especially the claim that no one saw him (90:7); the senses given by God make that boast untenable."}, {"id": "90:8/q01/p3", "position": "Its past tense points to gifts already given before the person became arrogant.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts the past construction with alam against lan, which projects the person's deluded claim that no one will ever overpower him into the future."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q02", "question": "What are the two eyes and what do they enable?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair denotes only the physical organs or also the heart's sight; Elmalılı expressly gives both possibilities.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q02/p1", "position": "They are the two bodily eyes that give sight of the visible world.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī explicitly calls them literal eyes. Al-Ṭabarī says they see God's proofs; al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and others say they see visible things. Al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān distinguish the tongue's expression and the lips' covering of the mouth and help with speech, eating, drinking and blowing. Al-Bursawī adds sight from earth to heaven, recognition of benefit and harm, and viewing the world, Qurʾān and divine signs. He describes the eye as an image-receiving mirror: small pupil, quick movement, lids and lashes protect it; eyes sit high like a beacon lamp, are paired like sun and moon, have dark brows and pupils to reduce glare, and black lashes that strengthen vision. His report relates black clothing to glare from white marble and says antimony strengthens sight. He says movable pupils see without neck movement and eyes at one level prevent double vision. Al-Biqāʿī says they form symmetrically in the womb's three darknesses, with varied colors and an inexplicable power of sight. Quṭb emphasizes their precise construction; al-Rāzī points to anatomy books for the extraordinary properties of bodily organs. Ibn Jurayj leaves further benefits unspecified as 'and so on.'"}, {"id": "90:8/q02/p2", "position": "The pair can also encompass outward sight and an inward eye of insight.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says the bodily eye sees signs of divine workmanship while the heart's eye sees loci of the unseen. Al-Wāsiṭī distinguishes an eye for created things from a special eye perceiving the Creator. Al-Biqāʿī contrasts sensory sight and moral insight, which open desire for perceived good and escape from evil. Al-Bursawī says both outer and inner eyes should be guarded and binocular sight is more complete. Elmalılı offers the visible pair or one visible eye with the heart's eye as possibilities."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q03", "question": "Why are the eyes singled out?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q03/p1", "position": "Sight is especially useful and directly answers the claim that no one sees the person.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives both grounds: the eyes are the most useful of the senses, and their mention answers the preceding claim in 90:7."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q04", "question": "What lesson follows from God giving these faculties?", "turns_on": "The notes draw several complementary consequences from the gifts: gratitude, proof of divine power and knowledge, restraint, and moral choice.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q04/p1", "position": "The visible gifts call for reflection and gratitude to God.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly calls the eyes, tongue and lips evident, abundant or recurring blessings that God uses to remind people to give thanks; al-Thaʿlabī says they compel gratitude. Al-Baghawī says the enumeration calls the person to reflect. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls them blessings that establish proof against him. Al-Biqāʿī says the intricacy of the eyes and their formation in the womb call for gratitude. Al-Nasafī calls the eyes a favor, and Ibn Jurayj leaves other benefits implicit."}, {"id": "90:8/q04/p2", "position": "The maker of human perception can see, know, overpower, resurrect and reckon the person.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq and Ibn al-Jawzī invoke the eyes as signs of resurrection; al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī and Study Quran add reckoning. Al-Rāzī says the maker of rational heart and eloquent tongue from humble fluid can destroy creation and knows hidden things, removing excuse for denial or spending against religion. Al-Biqāʿī says the benefactor knows affairs and can bring benefit or harm, personally or through whomever He wills. Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes 67:14: the giver of knowledge cannot be ignorant or powerless. Al-Ḥasan frames the boast as a challenge to who will account for spending."}, {"id": "90:8/q04/p3", "position": "Sight and speech are entrusted for lawful, accountable use.", "reasons": "The reported address commands closing lids and lips against forbidden sight and speech and restraining sexual desire. Al-Biqāʿī urges lawful perception and avoidance of what God forbids. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ stresses accountable sight and words rather than mere anatomy shared with animals. Iṣlāḥī says wealth has distracted addressees from seeing the needy around them. Quṭb contrasts the gift of sight with boasting and withholding what God supplied. Al-Bursawī says the outward and inward eyes should both be guarded."}, {"id": "90:8/q04/p4", "position": "These senses equip people for knowledge, moral discernment and responsible choice.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says bodily faculties permit perfection, learning from lessons, asking and speaking before guidance to good and evil. Ibn ʿĀshūr presents a progression from senses that acquire knowledge, to speech that communicates it, to guidance that tests good and evil. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says innate discernment equips a human to bear the difficult trust. Kur'an Yolu links external knowledge to judgment of truth and falsehood and choice; it calls humans exceptional, responsible beings. Al-Ṭabarī specifically says the eyes see divine proofs."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q05", "question": "What does the reported divine address say about guarding the faculties?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q05/p1", "position": "God gave coverings or means of restraint, so people should close their eyes, lips and sexual organs against forbidden use.", "reasons": "The Prophet's report in al-Thaʿlabī speaks of two coverings each for tongue, eyes and private parts. Al-Baghawī describes lips, eyelids and other bodily means; his fuller version addresses Adam's child. Abū Ḥāzim's report in al-Qurṭubī specifies lips, eyelids and protective coverings against forbidden speech, sight and desire. Al-Durr's reports command lawful use and closing eyes against the forbidden; one adds that humans cannot bear God's anger or withstand His vengeance. These are var

{"id": "90:8/q06", "question": "How does this reminder answer the preceding claims and hardship?", "turns_on": "Which nearby human claim or statement the divine question answers: being unseen, being unconquerable, hardship, unbelief, or spending.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q06/p1", "position": "The giver of eyes must see and know the person who imagines no one sees him.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī make the created eyes answer the claim about being unseen. Al-Rāzī connects it to 90:7 as evidence of divine power; al-Bayḍāwī says the favor clarifies that warning. Al-Ālūsī adds God's capacity to requite and account. Elmalılı asks whether the maker of sight could fail to see deeds. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates both seeing and overpowering claims to God's creation of perception and speech and cites 67:14. Al-Sāmarrāʾī calls the response direct. Study Quran draws accountability for the faculties' use."}, {"id": "90:8/q06/p2", "position": "The creator of the organs can overpower the one who claims nobody can overpower him.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī link this to 90:5: God made the eyes that see proofs and the organs that speak. Al-Rāzī's fuller excerpt says eyes, tongue, lips and guidance display divine power against the boast. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the maker of perception and speech cannot be powerless; his fuller note invokes 67:14."}, {"id": "90:8/q06/p3", "position": "The faculties answer the account of human hardship by removing excuse during moral testing.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the senses accompany the hardship of responsibility. Al-Ṭabrisī explicitly connects this reading with 90:4: God tests by commands after equipping humanity. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the senses and innate discernment prepare a human to bear the difficult trust."}, {"id": "90:8/q06/p4", "position": "The wondrous capacities and guidance expose the unbeliever's own responsibility for unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this fourth connection: God made the body's capacities as evidence against the unbeliever and guided him, making his unbelief his own doing."}, {"id": "90:8/q06/p5", "position": "The maker of his organs can hold the boastful spender to account.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan takes the boast as asking who can account for expenditure; al-Rāzī reports the answer as the One who created the person's organs. Al-Rāzī also says divine knowledge of hidden things leaves no excuse for spending against God's religion."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q07", "question": "How do the eyes and other faculties lead into the two paths?", "turns_on": "Whether the following pair of paths denotes moral alternatives or the breasts that nourish a child; al-Qaffāl prefers the moral reading.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q07/p1", "position": "The two elevated paths are good and evil, made discernible to a morally equipped person.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī glosses najd as an elevated road and likens clear proofs to a high visible way; he says most exegetes take the paths as good and evil. Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying these are the roads of good and evil and one must not prefer evil. Al-Qaffāl prefers this interpretation. Al-Qāshānī, Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Kur'an Yolu relate sight, speech and moral awareness to distinguishing and choosing the paths; Kur'an Yolu adds true versus false and good versus bad. Al-Rāzī compares 76:2–3, where creation with hearing and sight is followed by guidance and grateful or ungrateful response. Ibn ʿĀshūr says senses acquire knowledge, speech communicates it and guidance distinguishes and tests good and evil."}, {"id": "90:8/q07/p2", "position": "The two elevated paths are a child's two breasts, supplying life and provision.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib; the two breasts are paths by which the child receives sustenance."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q08", "question": "How do the gifts prepare the later call to difficult deeds?", "turns_on": "The notes explain different stages in the sura's ethical progression from equipped perception to difficult action.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q08/p1", "position": "The endowed person is responsible for taking the steep path and serving people in need.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr says people have eyes and means of reflection yet fail to save themselves, directing attention to the challenge in 90:11. Corpus Coranicum says rhetorical questions turn to a categorical judgment that the person endowed with insight and choice fails the steep path. Iṣlāḥī traces 90:8–17 from sight, speech and moral awareness through freeing slaves, feeding the poor, faith, patience and compassion, as remedies for greed and service to God. He also says the wealthy have failed to use their eyes to see the needy. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says sight and speech prepare the warning about moral consequences, especially of words."}, {"id": "90:8/q08/p2", "position": "The hard path and service call for patience, then mercy and exhortation.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says choosing a path, climbing the ascent, freeing enslaved people, enduring famine and caring for orphans and the destitute all require perseverance. He says patience is mentioned first because of the earlier toil, ascent and two paths, and mercy follows the duties of freeing and feeding. Iṣlāḥī says exhortation is a believer's obligation and a virtuous deed remains incomplete without it."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q09", "question": "How is this verse arranged within the passage?", "turns_on": "The notes identify either the local stanza pattern or a parallel passage as the organizing connection.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q09/p1", "position": "It belongs to a second triplet of gifts within two rhymed triplets of polemical questions.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the second stanza resumes the introduction's statement about humanity; repeated third-person questions bind two triplets. The second triplet lists sight, speech and moral direction, recalling creation in 90:4; a rhyme shift accents the contrast with human self-importance."}, {"id": "90:8/q09/p2", "position": "The parallel account of creation joins senses to guidance and the possibility of gratitude or ingratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explicitly compares 76:2–3, which describes human creation with hearing and sight followed by guidance to two paths and a grateful or ungrateful response."}]}
{"id": "90:8/q10", "question": "What incidental excerpt material accompanies the verse?", "turns_on": "The two notes preserve different incidental content in the supplied excerpts and do not dispute one another.", "positions": [{"id": "90:8/q10/p1", "position": "One excerpt supplies only the verse text, without an explanation of it.", "reasons": "The al-Rāzī full-text segment contains the wording about eyes, tongue, lips and two paths but no commentary on those verses."}, {"id": "90:8/q10/p2", "position": "A lexical heading lists other senses of ghishiya without examples here.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī's excerpt also names elevation or riding over, drowsiness and darkness as senses of ghishiya, but does not exemplify them in the passage."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q01", "question": "What does Thamūd's denial through bi-ṭaghwāhā mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭaghwāhā denotes the people's culpable conduct, the calamity they denied, or the collective scope of the act; the punishment analysis also differs over an omitted genitive.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q01/p1", "position": "Their rebellion and disobedience drove them to deny the truth or their messenger.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Ibn Zayd gloss it as disobedience or transgression; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, and others make that rebellion the cause of denial. Ibn Kathīr says it fixed rejection of guidance and certainty in their hearts. Al-Biqāʿī specifies disbelief, sins, and oppression; Elmalılı says their strength as rock-cutters fed arrogance. Islahi says they rebelled after truth was clear. Corpus Coranicum contrasts 95:7 and 82:9, where the preposition supplies the object, and distinguishes the punishment at 69:5 from their disobedience here. Al-Qurṭubī says they exceeded bounds in disobedience; Qutb says tyranny hid guidance and defiled them. Al-Ṭabarī reports this view alongside his punishment interpretation."}, {"id": "91:11/q01/p2", "position": "They denied the promised, overwhelming punishment that struck them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names the punishment Ṭaghwā; al-Ṭabarī links it to al-ṭāghiya in 69:5. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī say an exceptional blast exceeds ordinary bounds and can thus be called transgressive, with al-Rāzī also citing 69:4. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says they denied it until it arrived. Al-Naḥḥās explains an omitted genitive, 'punishment of their ṭaghwā'; al-Ālūsī instead allows direct attachment without ellipsis and takes the verbal noun as intensifying the torment. Sources variously call it promised punishment, extraordinary cry, overpowering calamity, or immediate destruction."}, {"id": "91:11/q01/p3", "position": "The expression embraces all Thamūd's misdeeds or transgression collectively.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb's gloss varies among all reported meanings, all misdeeds together, all Thamūd collectively, and their collective transgression. Ibn Kathīr quotes 'all of them together.' These reports preserve the scope of 'all' without specifying a single particular act."}]}

Al-Wāḥidī's concise works say they denied the messengers; Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Kathīr, and the Study Quran identify the messenger as Ṣāliḥ or the prophet sent to them."}, {"id": "91:11/q02/p2", "po

Elmalılı says they rejected both the miraculous camel and the truthful warning; denying a true report is sin and denying a prophet's report is disbelief in the God who sent him."}, {"id": "91:11/q02/p3", "position": "They denied the punishment threatened against them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls ṭaghwā the name of that punishment; al-Ṭabarī relates it to 69:5. Al-Rāzī and al-Wāḥidī explain that an extraordinary blast exceeded ordinary bounds."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q03", "question": "Why is the verb feminine with Thamūd?", "turns_on": "Whether the feminine form is taken as expressive rhetoric or agreement with a tribe name.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q03/p1", "position": "The feminine form portrays the weak effect of Thamūd's denial.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says listeners can plainly recognize its injustice from the clear sign and ugly outcome."}, {"id": "91:11/q03/p2", "position": "Thamūd is treated grammatically as the name of a tribe.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts the feminine reference here with later plural pronouns referring to the people collectively."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q04", "question": "How is the bāʾ in bi-ṭaghwāhā construed?", "turns_on": "Whether bāʾ expresses cause, means, or the object of denial; the last analysis also turns on whether a genitive is omitted.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q04/p1", "position": "It marks the cause of denial: their rebelliousness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attribute this to most interpreters. Ibn ʿĀshūr equates the cause with extreme arrogance and compares Quraysh's pride, citing 2:15 and 43:31. Corpus Coranicum contrasts object-marking uses at 95:7 and 82:9. Al-Ālūsī judges the difference from the instrumental reading slight."}, {"id": "91:11/q04/p2", "position": "It is instrumental or metaphorically instrumental: they denied by means of rebellion.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī compares 'I wrote with a pen'; al-Samīn reports this as his first analysis. Al-Ālūsī says it differs little from causation."}, {"id": "91:11/q04/p3", "position": "It attaches to 'denied' as the punishment's complement.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī relate this to the overwhelming torment at 69:5. Al-Naḥḥās supplies 'punishment of their ṭaghwā' by ellipsis and compares asking a town for its people; al-Ālūsī says direct attachment requires no omitted genitive."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q05", "question": "What does ṭaghwā mean as an Arabic word?", "turns_on": "Whether the root's excess describes human disobedience or the exceptional punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q05/p1", "position": "It means transgression or tyranny beyond bounds, including disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Layth gives ṭughyā and ṭughwān as dialectal verbal nouns beside verbs ṭaghaytu and ṭaghawtu. Al-Zajjāj derives it from ṭughyān. Jishumī includes corruption and disobedience; al-Ālūsī calls it exceeding the limit in disobedience. Islahi specifies rebellion after truth is clear."}, {"id": "91:11/q05/p2", "position": "Here it is a name or description of the overwhelming punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names the punishment Ṭaghwā. Al-Rāzī says a cry exceeding normal bounds fits the root; al-Ṭabarī and others compare al-ṭāghiya at 69:5."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q06", "question": "How is the noun ṭaghwā formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the wāw is a change from yāʾ, an original dialectal root letter, or left unanalyzed.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q06/p1", "position": "It is a faʿlā verbal noun with yāʾ changed to wāw to distinguish noun from adjective.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq compare taqwā, khazyā, and daʿwā; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī likewise explain a yāʾ-root noun shifted to wāw. Al-Qurṭubī gives underlying ṭaghyāhā. Jishumī proposes derivation from ṭāghiya."}, {"id": "91:11/q06/p2", "position": "Its wāw may be original in a dialect using ṭaghawtu.", "reasons": "Al-Layth records both ṭaghaytu and ṭaghawtu. Abū al-Baqāʾ makes the wāw original for the latter speakers; al-Ālūsī cites al-Rāghib for both roots and says this removes the supposed irregularity of the ḍamma form."}, {"id": "91:11/q06/p3", "position": "It is simply a verbal noun equivalent to ṭughyān.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī treat both as verbal nouns; Ibn ʿAṭiyya does so without a root derivation. Al-Naḥḥās calls them synonyms."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q07", "question": "Why use ṭaghwā rather than ṭughyān or a yāʾ form?", "turns_on": "Whether verse-ending correspondence or the expressive force of wāw explains the chosen form.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q07/p1", "position": "The form fits the sūra's verse endings.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, and al-Qurṭubī connect the form to rhyme. They compare daʿwā from supplication and 10:10; al-Farrāʾ also cites final prayer there. Müller likewise calls it rhyme driven, while Corpus Coranicum notes other Quranic ṭughyān occurrences postdate this sūra."}, {"id": "91:11/q07/p2", "position": "The stronger wāw form underscores the extremity of denial.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī prefers the wāw for force and says it marks the extreme degree of their denial; he also distinguishes the fatḥa noun and ḍamma verbal noun."}]}
{"id": "91:11/q08", "question": "How is ṭaghwāhā read?", "turns_on": "The vowel on ṭāʾ and whether the ḍamma form is a dialectal verbal noun or morphologically irregular.", "positions": [{"id": "91:11/q08/p1", "position": "The common reading has fatḥa on ṭāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Samīn call this the general or majority reading; it is analyzed as a verbal noun, and al-Biqāʿī calls the fatḥa form a noun."}, {"id": "91:11/q08/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥasan and others read ṭughwāhā with ḍamma on ṭāʾ.", "reasons": "The named readers vary: Ḥammād is called ibn Salama or ibn Sulaymān; al-Jaḥdarī and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb are also listed. Sources treat the form as a dialect variant like fatwā/fitwā or a verbal noun like ʿuqbā, rujʿā, and ḥusnā. {"id": "91:13/q19", "question": "What inward meanings are given to the camel and her drink?", "turns_on": "Different allegorical correspondences.", "positions": [{"id": "91:13/q19/p1", "position": "The she-camel is the soul, a divine gift carrying a person through deeds; its water sustains remembrance and worship.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the soul must be preserved and purified; neglecting and slaughtering this gift merits destruction."}, {"id": "91:13/q19/p2", "position": "The camel is the spiritual path or way of law.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a larger scheme: sun as necessary existence or divine essence, brightness as first determination or existence, moon as fixed entities or first determination, day and night as manifestation or beauty and majesty, heaven and earth as subtle and dense worlds."}, {"id": "91:13/q19/p3", "position": "The camel and its drink are longing and remembrance or reflection.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a scheme with sun as divine essence, light as Muhammadan reality, moon as possible being, day as manifest world, night as contingent existence veiling the Real, heaven as intellect and earth as body."}]}
{"id": "91:13/q20", "question": "How does this account connect to other Quranic accounts of Thamūd?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:13/q20/p1", "position": "The brief account presumes fuller Quranic treatments of the camel's water share, warning, and punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the camel and drink have already been treated. {"id": "91:13/q22", "question": "How is this Quranic account related to a pre-Islamic poem?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:13/q22/p1", "position": "It recasts an older Thamūd story by adding a divine messenger and explicit command, turning consecrated-camel disrespect into a moral and theological warning.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum considers Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt's poem likely authentic: it lacks a divine warner, the foal's curse brings destruction, and its culprit Aḥmar may reflect overlapping traditions.
